name: So
confidence_why: Migliazza's 1998 reference grammar places stress on the final (major) syllable of the sesquisyllabic word with the minor presyllable unstressed, Lerthirunwong 1980 says the same for the same Kusuman variety, and Jungprasert 1986 agrees for the Dong Luang variety, differing only in giving full-vowel minor syllables a secondary stress.
catalog_citation: Migliazza, Brian. 1998. A grammar of So — a Mon-Khmer language of Northeast Thailand. PhD thesis, Mahidol University. xii+210 pp. ISBN 974-661-067-8. [Ch. II Phonology, secs. 2.1–2.3, pp. 31–32.] Restated verbatim in Migliazza, Brian. 2003. So Stories: a preliminary analysis of texts in a Mon-Khmer language. Mon-Khmer Studies 33: 67–158, at pp. 71–72.
catalog_locator: Thesis pp. 31–32: sec. 2.1 Introduction (p. 31), sec. 2.2 Stress (pp. 31–32, Figure 8), sec. 2.3 Syllable Patterns (p. 32). Same wording in Migliazza 2003 pp. 71–72, sec. B 'Overview of So phonology', subsections 'Stress' and 'Syllable patterns'.
catalog_quote: Stress placement is predictable occurring on the last syllable. Disyllabic words have a short minor presyllable consisting of CV(N) or a syllabic nasal N̩. ... 2.2 Stress. Most So words are monosyllabic. On disyllabic words, however, the stress is usually on the second (or major) syllable. The preceding short minor syllable is unstressed. That is, the phonological word is composed of: Phonological Word (PW) (σ) 'σ. Thus an optional unstressed preceding syllable (σ) may occur before the main stressed syllable ('σ). The following So examples reflect this disyllabic pattern of stress placement. The period (σ.σ) marks the boundary between syllables. ku.'ci:t die; ʔa.'ci:t to kill; ʔa.'baŋ to hide something; ma.'na:ŋ sun; pa.'ni̤c bamboo shoots; ra.'bɑh beak; tʰa.'nṳ: a bow (weapon); ta.'bɯ: evening; ba.'daŋ wonder; ca.'ri̤ak buffalo; ha.'mɑ how much; ci.'wa:c pull back; pʰa.'ɲa: word; sa.'bat transplant; si.'yɛ:ŋ kind of fish. 2.3 Syllable Patterns. Katuic languages (and many other Mon-Khmer languages) have a sesquisyllabic syllable type, in which there is an optional minor (pre-) syllable followed by a major stressed syllable. Thus So words are mostly monosyllabic (major syllable) or disyllabic (minor syllable plus a major syllable). So is predominantly sesquisyllabic with stress placement on the final syllable of the word. Historically, the final syllable is being progressively strengthened with a corresponding weakening of the non-final syllable (Thomas 1992).
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Words are monosyllables or sesquisyllables; in a disyllable the final (major) syllable carries the stress and the preceding minor presyllable (CV(N) or syllabic nasal, vowel restricted to /a i u/, clear register only) is unstressed and reduced. Stress is thus word-final and non-contrastive.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None mentioned (words are at most two syllables).
new_statements.exceptions: Hedged as 'usually' on the second syllable; no counter-examples given. Minor-syllable vowel shows free variation short~long. Lerthirunwong 1980:20 adds that a ʔaʔ presyllable may be dropped altogether, leaving a monosyllable.
new_statements.domain_note: Phonological word (citation forms); the language also has a two-way register (clear vs breathy phonation) contrast on the major syllable, not tone. Variety: So of Kusuman District, Sakon Nakhon (the prestige dialect on the Thai side). Same rule stated independently in Lerthirunwong 1980 sec. 0.8 (also Kusuman).
new_statements.identity_note: Both quoted sources describe the So (/thrò:/, autonym lakuay thro:) of Kusuman District, Sakon Nakhon Province, NE Thailand = Glottolog sooo1254 [sss]. Caution on Glottolog's bibliography for this languoid: per Migliazza 2003:69-70, Kulachol 1986 and Jungprasert 1986 ('So' of Dong Luang, Mukdahan) actually describe a Bru variety (Eastern/Western Bru, not sooo1254), and Suwilai 1996 'So (Thavung)' is Thavung (Vietic, thav1234), a different language altogether.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is predictable and falls on the last syllable of the word: words are monosyllables or sesquisyllables (optional short minor presyllable CV(N) or syllabic nasal + major syllable), and the major (final) syllable carries the stress while the minor presyllable is unstressed; PW = (σ) 'σ. Fifteen examples on p.32 (ku.'ci:t 'die', ʔa.'ci:t 'to kill', ca.'riak 'buffalo', ta.'bɯ: 'evening', etc.).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned; the minor presyllable is simply called unstressed.
new_statements.exceptions: None listed; the hedge 'usually on the second (or major) syllable' is not followed by any counterexample. Variety: So of Amphoe Kusuman, Sakon Nakhon (per the thesis abstract).
new_statements.identity_note: Migliazza 1998 describes So of Amphoe Kusuman, Sakon Nakhon (self-designation /tsro:/ per Jungprasert p.9). Jungprasert 1986 describes 'So (Bru)' of Ban Dong Luang, Amphoe Dong Luang, Mukdahan; its speakers call themselves /bru:/, the Thai call them So (pp.9, 196), and its phonology is taken from Darunee Kulachol 1986. Migliazza 2003:69-70 (noted) files the Dong Luang theses under Bru, not So; Glottolog files both under sooo1254. The stress facts are the same in both varieties.

new_statements.quote: There are three types of syllables in Dong Luang So: major syllables, minor syllables and presyllables. (1). Major Syllables. A major syllable is defined as a syllable which always takes primary stress. It can be either closed or open. [p.25] [...] (2). Minor Syllables. A minor syllable is defined as a syllable which take secondary stress. It may be a closed syllable or an open syllable. [p.26] [...] A presyllable with a pattern Cə is defined as a syllable which is formed by an initial consonant and a short open central vowel [ə]. It is always unstressed. The structure is Cə.(C(C)V(V)(C)(C)). [p.27] [...] A presyllable with a syllabic nasal consonant is defined as a syllable which is formed by a syllabic nasal consonant [m̩], [n̩] or [ŋ̍]. It is always unstressed. The structure is N.(C(C)V(C)(C)). [pp.27-28]

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement (primary stress on the final major syllable, preceding syllables weaker) as the catalog and as Migliazza 1998/2003 and Lerthirunwong 1980, but for the Dong Luang, Mukdahan variety whose speakers call themselves /bru:/ (thesis pp.9, 196) rather than the Kusuman /tsro:/ variety the catalog quotes describe; it adds secondary stress on full-vowel minor syllables and a three-way major / minor / presyllable distinction. Migliazza 2003:69-70 treats this thesis as describing Bru of Dong Luang rather than So proper; the author herself calls Kusuman So and Dong Luang So 'both dialects of So' (p.196).
new_statements.rule_in_words: The word is a major syllable optionally preceded by a minor syllable or a presyllable. The major syllable, always word-final, always takes primary stress; a full-vowel minor syllable C(C)V(C) before it takes secondary stress (/ki:ka:jʔ/ 'lazy', /lambʌ:/ 'convenient', /pruŋpri:/ 'fruitful'); a Cə presyllable (/pəde:ʔ/ 'salted fish', /tamɯŋ/ 'to listen', /canaj/ 'day') or a syllabic-nasal presyllable (/mpe:/ 'chili', /ncajh/ 'uncle, aunt', /ŋkan/ 'arm') is always unstressed. So primary stress is fixed on the final (major) syllable.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Yes: minor syllables (full-vowel C(C)V(C) syllables preceding the major syllable) 'take secondary stress'; Cə and syllabic-nasal presyllables are always unstressed. No stress marks are written in the transcriptions.
new_statements.exceptions: None. The only other prosodic remark found is sec. 9.5.1 (p.193): clause-level prominence by reduplication 'with/without an accompanying rising pitch on the first element', which is phrasal emphasis, not word stress.

tone_statements.citation: Chuenchom, Am-on (เอมอร ชื่นชม). 1999 [2542]. การศึกษาเปรียบเทียบคำศัพท์ภาษาโซ่ในจังหวัดสกลนคร จังหวัดนครพนม จังหวัดมุกดาหาร [A comparative study of lexical items of the So language in Sakon Nakhon, Nakhon Phanom and Mukdahan provinces]. MA thesis (Thai epigraphy), Silpakorn University, Bangkok.
tone_statements.quote: [p.26] ระบบเสียงของภาษาโซ่ที่ใช้พูดกันทั้ง 3 ถิ่น ประกอบด้วยหน่วยเสียง 3 ประเภท คือ หน่วยเสียงพยัญชนะ หน่วยเสียงสระ และลักษณะน้ำเสียง (Registers) [...] [p.43] ลักษณะน้ำเสียงภาษาโซ่ทั้ง 3 ถิ่นนั้นอธิบายได้ดังนี้ 1. ลักษณะน้ำเสียงปกติ (clear voice quality) ใช้แทนด้วยสัญลักษณ์ R1 เกิดกับระดับเสียง 2 ระดับ คือ ระดับเสียงสูง (high-rising pitches) และระดับเสียงกลาง (mid-level pitches) 1.1 ระดับเสียงสูง (high-rising pitches) จะเกิดกับพยางค์ปิดพยัญชนะท้ายเป็นเสียงกัก /p, t, k / และพยัญชนะท้ายเสียงแทรก / h / [...] 1.2 ระดับเสียงกลาง (mid-level pitches) จะเกิดกับพยางค์เปิดสระเสียงยาว และพยางค์ปิดที่พยัญชนะท้ายเป็นเสียงนาสิก / m, n, ɲ, ŋ / เสียงข้างลิ้นและเสียงลิ้นรัว / l, r / และเสียงกึ่งสระ / w, j / [...] 2. ลักษณะน้ำเสียงต่ำทุ้มมีลมควบคู่ (breathy-voice quality) ใช้สัญลักษณ์แทนด้วย R2 ซึ่งจะมีระดับเสียงต่ำตก (low-falling pitch) ลักษณะของ R2 นี้จะเกิดกับคำพยางค์เปิดและคำพยางค์ปิดที่เป็นทั้งสระเสียงสั้นและสระเสียงยาว รวมทั้งเกิดได้กับพยัญชนะท้ายได้ทุกตัว
tone_statements.translation: [p.26] The sound system of So as spoken in all 3 localities consists of 3 kinds of units: consonant phonemes, vowel phonemes and register (Registers). [...] [p.43] The registers of So in all 3 localities can be described as follows: 1. Normal (clear) voice quality, symbolised R1, occurs with 2 pitch levels, namely high pitch (high-rising pitches) and mid pitch (mid-level pitches). 1.1 The high (high-rising) pitch occurs with closed syllables whose final is a stop /p, t, k/ or the fricative /h/ [...] 1.2 The mid-level pitch occurs with open long-vowel syllables and with closed syllables ending in a nasal /m, n, ɲ, ŋ/, the lateral or trill /l, r/ or a semivowel /w, j/ [...] 2. The low, deep voice quality with accompanying breathiness (breathy-voice quality), symbolised R2, has low-falling pitch; R2 occurs with open syllables and with closed syllables with both short and long vowels, and can occur with every final consonant.
tone_statements.locator: thesis p.26 opening of 'ระบบเสียงภาษาโซ่'; pp.42-43 'ลักษณะน้ำเสียง (Register)' with ตารางที่ 3
tone_statements.summary: No lexical tone; two-way register (clear vs breathy) with predictable pitch: clear register high-rising in checked/-h syllables, mid-level elsewhere; breathy register low-falling.

tone_statements.citation: Miller, John D. and Carolyn P. Miller. 1994. Notes on phonology and orthography in several Katuic Mon-Khmer groups in Northeast Thailand. Mon-Khmer Studies 24: 27-51.
tone_statements.quote: In the following charts, second register refers to the lax, breathy register commonly found in Katuic languages and first register to the tense or non-breathy register. [...] In all dialects, second register vowels tend.to be higher in tongue height position (for the high and mid vowels) than do their first register counterparts, These second register high and mid vowels also have, to varying degrees, a lax or breathy quality. [...] All of the dialects studied demonstrate register contrast, though in differing degrees.
tone_statements.locator: p.34 (section 4, vowels/register), with 'All of the dialects studied..' at the foot of p.34; per-dialect detail for Pho Thi Phai San on p.35; So Kusuman identified as Ban Pho Thi Phai San on p.27
tone_statements.summary: No lexical tone described; two-way vocalic register (1st tense/modal vs 2nd lax/breathy with vowel-height/onglide correlates), weakly realised in So Kusuman (long vowels + short i); word stress not treated in the pages read.

tone_statements.citation: Kania, Raymond S. and Siriphan Hatuwong Kania. 1979. The So people of Kusuman, northeastern Thailand. Journal of the Siam Society 67(1): 74-110.
tone_statements.quote: The So language is a non-tonal, unwritten language belonging to the Mon-Khmer group of languages. [...] All of the acquired words are modified, some by sound, and all of them dispense with varying tones found in the Thai and Laotian languages. So words are usually of one or two syllables, but there are some with three. While stress can be on any syllable, it appears to be more common on the last. [...] [p.104] While there are no conjugations of verbs or tone marks in the So language, it is by no means an easy language to learn.
tone_statements.locator: p.103, first paragraph under 'Some characteristics of So pronunciation'; p.104 last paragraph before 'So folktales'. Extract
tone_statements.summary: Non-tonal (explicit); stress mostly on the last syllable.

tone_statements.quote: ส่วนสุริยา รัตนกุล (2531 : 142) กล่าวว่า พวกโส้อพยพจากประเทศลาว [...] กลุ่มชนชาวโส้ยังคงรักษาภาษาของเขาไว้ได้ส่วนมากและใช้ภาษาโส้ในการพูดจาติดต่อสื่อสารกัน และพบว่าภาษาโส้ใช้ระดับเสียงสูงต่ำ (pitch) ในภาษา แต่ยังไม่วิวัฒนาการเป็นระบบเสียวรรณยุกต์ ในขณะเดียวกันก็มีการใช้ลักษณะน้ำเสียง (register) ในภาษาด้วย
tone_statements.translation: Suriya Ratanakul (1988: 142) says that the So migrated from Laos [...] The So community has still largely kept its language and uses So to communicate, and it was found that the So language uses high-low pitch levels (pitch) in the language, but [this] has not yet developed into a tone system; at the same time voice-quality register (register) is also used in the language. ['ระบบเสียวรรณยุกต์' sic for 'ระบบเสียงวรรณยุกต์']
tone_statements.locator: paragraph ending the 'ตระกูลภาษา' section, immediately before the heading 'ภาษาพูด'
tone_statements.summary: Not tonal: pitch differences present but 'not developed into a tone system'; register (voice quality) contrast used.

readall_conflicts: No placement conflict: every opened source (Migliazza 1998 pp.31-32; Jungprasert 1986 pp.25-28; and the Migliazza 2003 and Lerthirunwong 1980 statements already held by the project) puts primary stress on the final, major syllable of the sesquisyllabic word, with any preceding syllable weaker. The only difference is one of detail: Migliazza 1998 calls the minor presyllable simply 'unstressed', whereas Jungprasert 1986 (following Darunee Kulachol 1986) distinguishes full-vowel minor syllables, which carry secondary stress, from Cə/syllabic-nasal presyllables, which are unstressed. The larger caveat is identity, not placement: Jungprasert describes the Dong Luang (Mukdahan) variety, self-designated /bru:/, which Migliazza 2003 regards as Bru rather than So of Kusuman.

On disyllabic [words] it is usually the second of the disyllabic forms which is stressed, [resulting] in the shortening of the unstressed first syllable. ku:ci:t -> kŭʔci:t "die". The disyllabic words having ʔaʔ as the first syllable may have to drop the first syllable, resulting in a monosyllabic form.' Also sec. 0.7 Register: two registers, clear (mid level pitch) vs breathy (low rising pitch).

tone.translation: [p.26] The sound system of So as spoken in all 3 localities consists of 3 kinds of units: consonant phonemes, vowel phonemes and register (Registers). [...] [p.43] The registers of So in all 3 localities can be described as follows: 1. Normal (clear) voice quality, symbolised R1, occurs with 2 pitch levels, namely high pitch (high-rising pitches) and mid pitch (mid-level pitches). 1.1 The high (high-rising) pitch occurs with closed syllables whose final is a stop /p, t, k/ or the fricative /h/ [...] 1.2 The mid-level pitch occurs with open long-vowel syllables and with closed syllables ending in a nasal /m, n, ɲ, ŋ/, the lateral or trill /l, r/ or a semivowel /w, j/ [...] 2. The low, deep voice quality with accompanying breathiness (breathy-voice quality), symbolised R2, has low-falling pitch; R2 occurs with open syllables and with closed syllables with both short and long vowels, and can occur with every final consonant.
tone.summary: No lexical tone; two-way register (clear vs breathy) with predictable pitch: clear register high-rising in checked/-h syllables, mid-level elsewhere; breathy register low-falling.

sources.citation: Kania, Raymond S. and Siriphan Hatuwong Kania. 1979. The So people of Kusuman, northeastern Thailand. Journal of the Siam Society 67(1): 74-110.
sources.quote: The So language is a non-tonal, unwritten language belonging to the Mon-Khmer group of languages. [...] All of the acquired words are modified, some by sound, and all of them dispense with varying tones found in the Thai and Laotian languages. So words are usually of one or two syllables, but there are some with three. While stress can be on any syllable, it appears to be more common on the last. [...] [p.104] While there are no conjugations of verbs or tone marks in the So language, it is by no means an easy language to learn.
sources.locator: p.103, first paragraph under 'Some characteristics of So pronunciation'; p.104 last paragraph before 'So folktales'. Extract
sources.note: Section 'Language and folktales / Some characteristics of So pronunciation' (p.103): states outright that So is 'a non-tonal, unwritten language' of the Mon-Khmer group, that Thai/Lao loans 'dispense with varying tones', that words are mostly mono- or disyllabic and that stress 'can be on any syllable' but is 'more common on the last'; c. 40 phonemes (26 consonants, 14 vowels). p.104: 'no conjugations of verbs or tone marks in the So language'. A lay (non-linguist) description; register/phonation is not mentioned.

sources.note: Section 'ตระกูลภาษา': citing สุริยา รัตนกุล (2531 [1988]: 142) it says So 'uses high-low pitch levels (pitch) in the language, but this has not yet developed into a tone (วรรณยุกต์) system, while at the same time register (ลักษณะน้ำเสียง) is also used'. Under 'ภาษาพูด' an interviewed local teacher (ไกรสร ฮาดคะดี, 2019) gives 22 initials, 14 single finals, 3 cluster finals, 22 monophthongs, 5 diphthongs and says normal vs 'heavy' voice quality (น้ำเสียงปกติ/น้ำเสียงหนัก) is written with mai tho. Secondary compilation; the pitch remark is second-hand from Suriya 1988.
